opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting open problems, but I'm a bit cautious about the timeline. When people say "continual learning," they often mean different things. One version is just updating a model regularly with new data, and we already do that in a sense with each new release, or with fine-tuning and retrieval to keep knowledge current. The harder version is a model that keeps learning from its own interactions, in deployment, without a human-curated training run in between, and reliably gets better rather than worse.

The core technical challenge is still catastrophic forgetting. When you update the weights on new information, you tend to degrade things the model was good at before. There are mitigations, like mixing in replay data, parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA where you isolate updates, regularization approaches, or keeping a frozen base and layering adapters on top. They help, but none of them fully solve it at the scale and generality we'd want.

Then there's the reliability question, which I think is even bigger. If a model improves itself from its own outputs or from user feedback, how do you make sure the signal is actually good? We've seen that training on self-generated data can lead to drift or collapse if you're not careful. Where self-improvement has worked well recently is in domains with verifiable rewards, like math and code, where you can check whether an answer is correct. That's why reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has been so productive for reasoning models. Extending that to open-ended domains where correctness is fuzzy is much harder.

There's also a practical side. Companies want predictable, tested models. A model whose weights shift every day is hard to evaluate, hard to make safe, and hard to debug. So I suspect in the near term we'll see more of a hybrid approach: the base model stays fairly stable, while memory, retrieval, and tool use handle the "learning" at the system level, plus periodic, carefully curated updates to the weights.

So my overall take is cautiously optimistic. I think we'll see steady progress, especially in verifiable domains and with better memory mechanisms, but truly autonomous, reliable self-improvement in the weights is still a research problem rather than something I'd expect to see deployed broadly very soon.

r001.rationale: It calls reliable self-improvement in model weights a research problem, but does not clearly state that no pathway is currently known.

r002.rationale: It says regular updates with new data already occur through new releases and fine-tuning, and contrasts autonomous learning with human-curated training runs.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the cost or feasibility of maintaining a separate flagship model for each user.

r004.rationale: It discusses memory, retrieval, and tool use at the system level, but does not say continual learning requires models to run on personal devices.

r005.rationale: It mentions evaluation, safety, and debugging challenges from shifting weights, but not a bad shared-model update disrupting service for all users.

r006.rationale: It identifies reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards as productive, but does not describe it as continuously running or as continual learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I get asked a lot, and I think I'm honestly a bit more skeptical than most people on this one, or at least more cautious.

So let me first separate a few things, because "continual learning" gets used for very different ideas. One version is: can we keep updating the weights of a model over time as new data comes in, without having to retrain from scratch? And the other version, the one that gets people really excited, is this self-improvement loop, where the model generates its own training signal and gets better on its own.

On the first one, the pure continual pretraining or fine-tuning question, I'd say the prospects are actually decent, but it's still mostly an engineering problem. The core issue hasn't really gone away, which is catastrophic forgetting. If you keep training on new data, you degrade performance on things the model previously knew. There are a bunch of techniques that help: replay buffers where you mix in old data, parameter-efficient methods like LoRA adapters that you can swap in and out, lower learning rates, regularization approaches. And in practice a lot of what labs do is just periodic retraining with a refreshed data mix, which is kind of the boring answer. But it works, and I think that's where most of the practical value is right now.

The self-improvement story is where I get more careful. The thing people point to is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, the stuff that made the reasoning models work. And it really does work, but I think it's important to be precise about why. It works in domains like math and code because you have an external verifier. You can check if the answer is correct, you can run the unit tests. The model isn't really grading itself; the environment is grading it. So the signal comes from outside.

Once you remove that verifier and ask the model to judge its own outputs, you run into a pretty fundamental problem. The model's ability to evaluate is correlated with its ability to generate. If it has a blind spot, it will have that same blind spot as a judge. So you can get these loops where the model becomes more confident, more consistent with itself, but not actually more correct. And there's the model collapse concern too, where training on your own synthetic outputs narrows the distribution over time. I don't think that's as apocalyptic as some of the early papers suggested, because in practice you filter and you mix in real data, but it's a real pressure you have to actively counteract.

The other piece people underestimate is evaluation. If a model is updating itself continuously, you need to know whether it actually got better, and our benchmarks are pretty saturated and pretty gameable. If you can't measure reliably, you can't have reliable continual learning, almost by definition. I'd say that's the actual bottleneck more than any algorithmic trick.

So where do I land? I think we'll see steady progress on narrow, verifiable domains, and models will increasingly be used to generate and filter training data for the next generation, which is a kind of slow, offline self-improvement with humans in the loop. That's already happening. What I'm skeptical of is the fully autonomous, online version where a deployed model just keeps getting smarter on its own without a strong external grounding signal. I don't see a mechanism for that yet that doesn't eventually drift. And honestly, from a safety and reproducibility standpoint, I'm not sure we want that, because a model whose weights are changing in production is very hard to debug or audit.

So, cautiously optimistic on the mundane version, and I'd push back a bit on the hype around the recursive version.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic about continual learning, but I think the word “reliable” is doing a lot of work here. Getting a model to update from new data is one problem. Making sure that update actually improves the model, without degrading capabilities it already has, is a much harder problem.

And I would distinguish learning from new information from improving yourself using your own outputs. If a model generates an answer and then trains on that answer, there isn’t necessarily any new signal there. It can reinforce a mistake just as easily as reinforce something useful. You need some way to check the result. With code, for example, you can run tests. For more open-ended questions, that feedback is much harder to obtain.

So I think we’ll see progress first in constrained settings where there’s a useful feedback signal and we can evaluate the updates carefully. I’m less confident about a model that learns continuously from every interaction and autonomously decides which changes are improvements. The challenge isn’t just making it learn—it’s knowing what it should learn, what it should retain, and whether the change was actually beneficial.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic, but I think we have to separate a few things. Continual learning means the model can learn something new without losing capabilities it already has. Improving itself adds another challenge: how does it know that what it’s learning is actually correct?

If a model generates its own training data, it can reinforce its own mistakes. You need some feedback signal you can trust. With coding, for example, you can run tests. But for an open-ended answer, evaluating whether it’s better is much harder.

There’s also catastrophic forgetting. Updating a model on new information can make it worse at something else, so you need to evaluate both what it gained and what it lost.

I think we’ll see progress first in constrained settings where the feedback is clear and improvements can be checked. A general-purpose model that reliably improves itself from arbitrary interactions is a much harder problem. I’m optimistic about the direction, but I wouldn’t consider that solved.
